questions: If a cell is already painted black (#), must it remain black in the final configuration, or can it be repainted?
Are cells marked with a dot (.) considered already painted white and therefore fixed, or can they be changed to black?
Can cells marked with a question mark (?) be painted either black or white arbitrarily, or are there any restrictions on their final color?
Must the rectangle of black cells be non-empty, i.e., contain at least one cell, or is an empty rectangle (no black cells) allowed?
If the black cells form a rectangle, does the rectangle have to be axis-aligned with the grid rows and columns, or can it be any shape?
In the case where multiple rectangles could satisfy the conditions, is any such rectangle acceptable, or is there a preferred one (e.g., minimal area)?
Should the output be exactly "Yes" and "No" with that capitalization and no extra whitespace or newline characters?
Are there any constraints on the time or memory limits that could affect the choice of algorithm for the given limits (H, W ≤ 1000)?

inline_prompts: You are given a grid of H rows and W columns. Let (i,j) denote the cell at row i (1 \leq i \leq H) from the top and column j (1 \leq j \leq W) from the left. The state of the grid is represented by H strings S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_H, each of length W. Takahashi wants to paint each not-yet-painted cell white or black so that all the black cells form a rectangle. Note that the rectangle must have at least one row and one column. Determine whether this is possible. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: H W S_1 S_2 \vdots S_H Output If it is possible to paint all the not-yet-painted cells so that the black cells form a rectangle, print Yes; otherwise, print No. Constraints - 1 \leq H, W \leq 1000 - H and W are integers. - Each S_i is a string of length W consisting of #, ., ?. - There is at least one cell that is already painted black.
